statement: Some people think that the spread of multinational companies and global brands brings significant benefits to developing countries. Others believe that it damages local businesses and traditional ways of life.
question: Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.
model:
From fast-food chains to smartphone manufacturers, multinational corporations now operate in almost every corner of the globe. Whether their arrival enriches or harms poorer nations is fiercely contested, and in my opinion the answer depends largely on how firmly host governments regulate them.

Supporters of globalisation stress the economic opportunities that foreign companies create. When a car maker or electronics firm builds a factory, it brings jobs, investment and, crucially, expertise that local workers can later apply elsewhere. Vietnam offers a striking example: the arrival of major technology manufacturers over the past two decades has helped lift millions of people out of poverty and transformed the country into a significant exporter. Consumers also gain access to a wider range of products, often of higher and more consistent quality.

Critics, however, see a darker side. Small family-run shops and restaurants frequently cannot compete with the purchasing power and advertising budgets of international chains, and once they close, the profits that might have circulated within the community flow abroad instead. There is also a cultural cost. As high streets from Lima to Jakarta fill with the same logos, local cuisine, crafts and customs risk being displaced by a homogeneous global consumer culture, particularly among young people who associate foreign brands with status.

My own view is that these concerns are serious but not inevitable. Countries can welcome foreign investment while requiring firms to train local staff, source materials from domestic suppliers and respect environmental standards. At the same time, governments can protect cultural heritage by supporting traditional markets and promoting local products, so that global and local businesses coexist rather than one replacing the other.

In conclusion, multinational companies can be a powerful engine of development, yet they can also undermine local economies and identities. Wise regulation, rather than either blind acceptance or outright rejection, is the key to ensuring that their presence is beneficial.
